steps.say: In this wall defect the bowel floats outside the belly with no covering sac at all, always to the right of a normal umbilical cord. The exposed loops stew in amniotic fluid for months, turning thick, swollen and inflamed. The cord itself is intact, which separates this defect from its covered cousin.
steps.tx: **Gastroschisis** (uncovered wall defect) always lies right of an intact cord at the obliterated right **umbilical vein** (sealed cord vessel), has no sac, and exposes bowel to **amniotic fluid** (womb water) causing thickening, edema and inflammation. The intact cord with free-floating bowel is the bedside diagnosis.

steps.say: The hole is small, usually four centimetres, yet the bowel outside dwarfs it. One baby in seven carries a sealed segment of bowel alongside the defect, while the major syndromes that haunt the covered defect are strikingly absent here. The exposed loops thicken in the womb fluid, which complicates the later repair.
steps.tx: The fascial defect is typically **4** (four) cm, **intestinal atresia** (sealed bowel) complicates up to **15** (fifteen) percent, but other major **associated anomalies** (linked defects) are rare unlike **omphalocele** (covered sac defect). Isolated bowel injury dominates the outlook rather than syndromes. The exposed loops thicken from urine and stool in the fluid, complicating later **repair** (surgical closure).

steps.say: From the delivery room the bowel rides in a warm salty bag, hanging to the nipple line. This simple cover limits heat and fluid loss while the team inspects every loop, watching for twists. No attempt is made to push bowel back at the bedside.
steps.tx: After birth the infant goes into a warm saline filled **bowel bag** (protective pouch) to the **nipple line** (upper-chest level) to limit heat and fluid loss while allowing inspection and detection of twisting. Rough handling or premature reduction risks **volvulus** (bowel twist) and compartment injury.

steps.say: The composite drawing compares all three newborn wall defects at a glance: the hole in the diaphragm with its small lung, the covered midline sac, and the uncovered bowel to the right of the cord. Matching the baby to one panel fixes the diagnosis and the plan. Covered sac defects carry anomaly rates near half, while uncovered defects rarely do.
steps.tx: **Diaphragmatic hernia** (chest-wall hole) with **pulmonary hypoplasia** (small lung), covered **omphalocele** (sac-covered defect), and uncovered **gastroschisis** (free bowel) panel the differential. Covered sac with cord entering the sac means omphalocele; free bowel right of a normal cord means gastroschisis. Covered sac defects carry anomaly rates near half, while uncovered defects rarely do, so the panel also teaches **prognosis** (expected outlook).

steps.say: Half to four fifths of babies accept all the bowel back in one sitting without dangerous pressure. The rest receive a transparent silo stitched to the defect edge, with a little more bowel eased inside each day until skin and fascia close. Patience here prevents the belly becoming a pressure chamber.
steps.tx: **Primary reduction** (single-sitting closure) succeeds in **50** (fifty) to **80** (eighty) percent without excess tension, failures get a ringed **silo** (staged pouch) for **staged closure** (gradual shut) with gradual bedside reduction over days then fascial and skin closure. Safe closure respects **intraabdominal pressure** (belly pressure) limits.

steps.say: Pressure inside the closed belly is watched like a hawk. Beyond fifteen millimetres of mercury the kidneys, lungs and gut all suffer, which is compartment syndrome. The stitch-free option covers the reduced bowel with a clear waterproof dressing changed on day four. Too much tension means going back to the silo rather than forcing the belly shut.
steps.tx: Safe **intraabdominal pressure** (belly pressure) stays under **15** (fifteen) mm Hg to avoid **compartment syndrome** (pressure injury), and **sutureless closure** (dressing-only cover) covers reduced bowel and cord with a watertight clear dressing changed at **4** (four) days. Excess tension is released by returning to **silo reduction** (staged pouch closure) rather than forcing closure.

steps.say: When a sealed segment accompanies the defect, the wall closes first and the bowel waits. Inflamed thick bowel sewn too early leaks, so the join is postponed six to eight weeks until the loops soften. Feeds meanwhile run through the drip. Dye studies map the sealed segment before the delayed join is attempted.
steps.tx: With coexisting **atresia** (sealed bowel) the wall closes first in a **staged repair** (two-part plan) and bowel repair waits **6** (six) to **8** (eight) weeks because **bowel inflammation** (swollen gut) forbids immediate **anastomosis** (surgical join). **Parenteral nutrition** (drip feeds) bridges the wait while inflammation settles. Contrast studies map the sealed segment before the delayed **anastomosis** (surgical join).

steps.say: Recovery is measured in weeks, not days. One baby in five develops the premature gut infection after repair, most endure long sleepy bowel and liver strain from drip feeds, and undescended testes in one to two in ten are simply pushed back at closure without formal fixation. The navel hernia drawing shows the mildest cousin of these defects for comparison.
steps.tx: Late **necrotising enterocolitis** (gut infection) follows repair in up to **20** (twenty) percent, most infants endure prolonged **ileus** (sleepy bowel) and **cholestasis** (liver strain) from parenteral nutrition, and **undescended testis** (high testis; undescended testes) in **10** (ten) to **20** (twenty) percent are pushed back without formal **orchidopexy** (testis fixation) at closure. Large defects accept **prosthetic patch** (synthetic cover) with skin cover, and testes left inside usually complete **testicular descent** (scrotal drop) spontaneously. An **umbilical hernia** (navel bulge) is the mild self-closing cousin.
